questions.questionText: What problem does splitting one overloaded agent into multiple specialized agents typically solve?
options: It makes the system cheaper to run in every case
A single agent with too many tools and instructions tends to get worse at all of them, since everything competes for the same prompt
It removes the need for tool descriptions
It eliminates the need for a control loop entirely
questions.correctAnswer: A single agent with too many tools and instructions tends to get worse at all of them, since everything competes for the same prompt
questions.explanation: A long, do-everything prompt makes it easy for instructions meant for one task to bleed into and confuse another; narrower, focused agents avoid this.

questions.questionText: In the supervisor pattern, what is the supervisor's job?
options: To do all the actual work itself
To decide which specialized worker agent should handle the request next, rather than doing the work directly
To replace the need for any worker agents
To only run once at the very start of the graph
questions.correctAnswer: To decide which specialized worker agent should handle the request next, rather than doing the work directly
questions.explanation: The supervisor's conditional edge routes to whichever specialized subgraph (worker) is appropriate — it's a routing decision-maker, not a doer.

questions.questionText: What's a real cost of splitting a single agent into a multi-agent system?
options: There is no cost, more agents are strictly better
More agents means more LLM calls (cost/latency) and a harder system to debug — worth it only when a single agent's tools/instructions would otherwise conflict
Multi-agent systems require a different LLM provider
questions.correctAnswer: More agents means more LLM calls (cost/latency) and a harder system to debug — worth it only when a single agent's tools/instructions would otherwise conflict
questions.explanation: Splitting adds real overhead; the case for it is strongest when a single well-scoped agent genuinely can't handle the combined task well.
